chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Anatomy of Agricultural Seasonality

lessons.title: Why Agri Commodities Move on a Calendar, Not a News Cycle

body.text: An agri commodity's price is scheduled months in advance by its sowing-to-harvest calendar. Read the calendar first, then read the news.

children.text: Open a terminal on any trading day and the Nifty is reacting to an RBI policy call, a Fed statement, or an IT major's quarterly numbers. Open a chart for chana or soybean futures on NCDEX and a very different rhythm shows up: prices tend to soften every year around the same two or three months, then firm up again a few months later, almost regardless of what the news cycle is doing that week. That is not a coincidence and it is not a chart pattern in the technical analysis sense. It is the sowing to harvest calendar of the crop showing up directly in the price. This lesson builds the mental model for why that happens, before Chapter 2 shows you how to actually measure it.
Three Fixed Points on Every Crop's Calendar

Every crop that trades on NCDEX or MCX moves through the same three phases each cycle: sowing, when farmers commit land and money to the crop and supply for the season is effectively locked in; the growing window, when weather risk (monsoon rainfall, temperature, pest attacks) can still swing the eventual output; and harvest arrivals, when the crop physically reaches mandis and warehouses over a concentrated few weeks. Nothing in this cycle is optional or news driven. A soybean plant sown in June in Madhya Pradesh will be ready in October, not September and not December, whichever news channel is running that week.

body.caption: Sowing and harvest windows for major Indian agri commodities traded on NCDEX/MCX

body.text: Kharif and Rabi crops sit on opposite halves of the calendar. A kharif crop like soybean is scarcest in July-August, when last year's stock is running low and this year's harvest has not arrived, and most abundant right after its October-November harvest. A rabi crop like chana does the opposite: scarcest around September-October and most abundant after its February-March harvest. A portfolio holding both is exposed to two calendars pulling in different directions through the year.

children.text: Why the Calendar Repeats in the Price: Glut and Scarcity

markDefs.definition: A regulated wholesale market, typically an APMC (Agricultural Produce Market Committee) yard, where farmers sell their harvest to traders, processors and commission agents. This is where spot agri prices in India are actually discovered, well before any of that produce reaches a futures screen.

children.text: The mechanism behind this is ordinary supply and demand, just compressed into a predictable few weeks instead of spread evenly across the year. When a harvest arrives, thousands of farmers across a growing belt bring their produce to

within a short window, because the crop ripens at roughly the same time everywhere in that agro-climatic zone. Warehouses fill up, arrivals data spikes, and spot prices typically soften as sellers outnumber immediate buyers. As the months pass, that harvested stock gets consumed, processed or exported, and by the time the next sowing season approaches, available stock is at its thinnest. Prices firm up into that scarcity, right up until the next harvest resets the cycle. This is why a trader in Indore watching soybean arrivals data, or an NCDEX chana trader watching sowing progress out of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, is often better positioned on seasonality than someone watching only the futures price ticker.

children.text: Why This Doesn't Happen to Equities or Gold

columns.label: Agri Commodities (Soybean, Chana, Cotton)
points: A fixed, repeating sowing-to-harvest calendar that is nearly identical year to year
Monsoon rainfall and weather during the growing window
Season-linked government policy: MSP announcements, import or export duty changes, stock limits
Physical arrivals data at mandis, which spikes in a predictable window every year

columns.label: Equities and Gold (Nifty, Infosys, Gold)
points: Quarterly earnings, guidance and management commentary, which reset every quarter, not on a fixed annual clock
RBI policy, Fed policy and global risk sentiment
Company-specific news: orders won, leadership changes, regulatory action
No physical harvest or arrivals event to anchor a repeating calendar

children.text: None of this means agri prices ignore news. A sudden export ban, an unexpected drought, or a surprise MSP hike can override the seasonal pattern completely, and Chapter 2 covers exactly when that happens. The point for now is narrower: before you explain any move in an agri commodity's price with a news headline, check whether the calendar already explains most of it.

body.title: Before You Call a Price Move "News Driven"
steps: Check which season the crop belongs to (Kharif or Rabi) and where you are in its sowing-to-harvest cycle
Pull up mandi arrivals data for the crop, available on Agmarknet or the NCDEX website, to see if arrivals are unusually high or low for this time of year
Compare the current month's price to that crop's typical seasonal pattern over the last 5 to 10 years
Only after doing the above, look for a genuine trigger (policy change, export ban, weather shock) that would explain a deviation from the seasonal pattern

body.title: Read the Calendar Before the Headline
body.scenario: It is the last week of September. Chana futures on NCDEX have risen about 6% over the past month, and a financial news channel is running a segment on "chana prices rally on strong festive demand." You are deciding whether this is a genuine opportunity or a routine seasonal move.
body.prompt: Before accepting the festive-demand explanation, what is the first thing you check, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Check where September falls in chana's own calendar first. Chana is a Rabi crop: sown around October-November and harvested in February-March. By late September, the previous February's harvest stock has been running down for roughly seven months, so this is close to the seasonally thinnest part of the year for old-crop stock, right before fresh sowing begins. A 6% rise in this window is close to what ordinary seasonal scarcity would produce even with completely flat demand. Festive demand may be adding to it, but the calendar likely explains most of the move on its own, which does not mean the news story is wrong, only that its actual contribution may be far smaller than the headline suggests.

body.text: Seasonality is a tendency built from many past cycles, not a guarantee for any single year. A drought, an unexpected import duty cut, or a bumper crop can push a commodity's price the opposite way from what the calendar alone would suggest. Treat everything in this chapter as the base case you adjust away from, not a fixed rule.

The crop calendars, price patterns and figures in this lesson are illustrative and for educational purposes only. They are not investment advice or a trading recommendation for any specific contract. Sowing and harvest windows shift with weather and region, so always verify current-year data against Agmarknet, NCDEX/MCX circulars and Ministry of Agriculture advisories before trading.

points: Every agri commodity traded on NCDEX or MCX moves through a fixed cycle, sowing, growing window, harvest arrivals, and that cycle repeats at roughly the same calendar months every year

Kharif crops (soybean, cotton) are sown around June-July and harvested October to January; Rabi crops (chana, mustard) are sown October-November and harvested February-March, opposite halves of the calendar
Prices tend to soften around harvest arrivals as supply floods mandis, then firm up as that stock is consumed through the year, tightest just before the next harvest
Equities and gold don't have this fixed physical calendar; their price drivers, earnings, policy, sentiment, reset every quarter or every news cycle instead
Always check where a crop sits in its own seasonal calendar before attributing a price move entirely to news; Chapter 2 shows how to test whether a seasonal pattern is statistically real
